arXiv:2508.13149v3 [cond-mat.mes-hall] 20 Apr 2026

Exchange Interactions of a Wigner Crystal in a Magnetic Field and Berry Curvature:
Multi-Particle Tunneling through Complex Trajectories

Preprint: APS/123-QED
Kyung-Su Kim Affiliation: kyungsu@illinois.edu Affiliation: Department of Physics and Anthony J. Leggett Institute for Condensed Matter Theory, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, 1110 West Green Street, Urbana, Illinois 61801, USA
August 24, 2026
Abstract

We study how an out-of-plane magnetic field B⁡(r)B(\textbf{r}) and a Berry curvature Ω⁡(k)\Omega(\textbf{k}) modify the exchange interactions in a two-dimensional Wigner crystal (WC) using a semiclassical large-rsr_{s} expansion. When only a magnetic field is present, ring-exchange processes arise from multi-particle tunneling through complex trajectories which constitute complex instanton solutions of the coordinate-space path integral. To leading order in BB, each exchange constant JaJ_{a} acquires an Aharonov-Bohm phase along the zero-field tunneling trajectory. When a Berry curvature is present, the multi-particle tunneling must be considered in a complexified phase space (r,k)(\textbf{r},\textbf{k}). To leading order in Ω\Omega, JaJ_{a} acquires a Berry phase along a purely imaginary momentum-space trajectory. When BB and Ω\Omega are both present, in addition to having both Aharonov-Bohm and Berry phases, the exchange magnitude |Ja||J_{a}| is also exponentially modified due to an effective-mass renormalization. These effects could be relevant for the WC and proximate phases recently observed in rhombohedral multilayer graphene.

I Introduction

The two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG)—Coulomb-interacting electrons confined to move in two dimensions—is governed by the dimensionless parameter rsr_{s} characterizing the ratio of interaction to kinetic energy

H0\displaystyle H_{0} =∑ipi22​m+∑i<je24​π​ϵ​1|ri−rj|,\displaystyle=\sum_{i}\frac{\textbf{p}_{i}^{2}}{2m}+\sum_{i<j}\frac{e^{2}}{4\pi\epsilon}\frac{1}{|\textbf{r}_{i}-\textbf{r}_{j}|}, (1)
rs\displaystyle r_{s} =e2/8​π​ϵ​r0ℏ2/2​m​r02=r0/aB.\displaystyle=\frac{e^{2}/8\pi\epsilon r_{0}}{\hbar^{2}/2mr_{0}^{2}}=r_{0}/a_{\rm B}. (2)

Here, r0=1/π​nr_{0}=1/\sqrt{\pi n} is the average interparticle distance (for an electron density nn) and aB=4​π​ϵ​ℏ2/m​e2a_{\mathrm{B}}={4\pi\epsilon\hbar^{2}}/{me^{2}} is the effective Bohr radius. The 2DEG forms a Fermi liquid (FL) for rs≪1r_{s}\ll 1 (weak-coupling regime) and a Wigner crystal (WC) for rs≫1r_{s}\gg 1 (strong coupling) [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] [6].

The magnetism within each such phase of the 2DEG is an interesting and subtle problem that has attracted long-standing attention [2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 9]. In particular, in the WC phase, the magnetism is determined by various multi-spin ring-exchange processes [10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17] (see [18] for the most recent study). The effective spin Hamiltonian is written as a sum over various ring-exchange interactions:

where PaP_{a} refers to an nan_{a}-particle exchange that permutes spins in each polygon in (3) in a counter-clockwise direction and (−1)Pa=(−1)na+1(-1)^{P_{a}}=(-1)^{n_{a}+1} is the sign of the permutation. 𝒫^a\mathcal{\hat{P}}_{a} is the permutation operator for PaP_{a}, which could in turn be expressed in terms of spins S [as in (24-28)]. JaJ_{a} is the exchange constant for PaP_{a} that is in general complex when the magnetic field BB or Berry curvature Ω\Omega is present (Ja∗J_{a}^{*} is the complex conjugate). When B=Ω=0B=\Omega=0, the semiclassical large-rsr_{s} approximation gives [13, 15, 14, 18]

Ja​[B=0,Ω=0]=Ja(0)​(Eh,rs)≡Eh​Aa(0)​S~a(0)rs5/4​2​π​e−rs​S~a(0),J_{a}[B=0,\!\Omega\!=\!0]=J_{a}^{(0)}(E_{h},r_{s})\equiv E_{h}\frac{A_{a}^{(0)}\!\sqrt{\!\tilde{S}_{a}^{(0)}}\!}{r_{s}^{5/4}\!\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\sqrt{r_{s}}\tilde{S}_{a}^{(0)}}\!, (4)

where Eh≡e24​π​ϵ​aBE_{h}\equiv\frac{e^{2}}{4\pi\epsilon a_{\rm B}} is the effective Hartree energy. S~a(0)\tilde{S}_{a}^{(0)} and Aa(0)A_{a}^{(0)} are, respectively, the normalized action and fluctuation determinant shown in Table 1.

How does an out-of-plane magnetic field B⁡(r)B(\textbf{r}) and a Berry curvature Ω⁡(k)\Omega(\textbf{k}) affect these exchange interactions? We address this in a 2DEG with a (possibly non-uniform) B⁡(r)B(\textbf{r}) 11 1 B⁡(r)B(\textbf{r}) can also be regarded as an emergent magnetic field arising from topologically non-trivial spin or pseudo-spin texture in a real space, as discussed in [60]. The spatial modulation of B⁡(r)B(\textbf{r}) at microscopic WC lattice scale is natural in this setting. and/or Ω⁡(k)\Omega(\textbf{k}) inherited from the parent Bloch band. Throughout this paper, we assume a small effective gg-factor (g≪1g\ll 1) and ignore Zeeman splitting [20]. Working deep in a WC regime (large rsr_{s}), we derive the asymptotic expression for JaJ_{a} for three settings: (i) B≠0B\neq 0 and Ω=0\Omega=0; (ii) B=0B=0 and Ω≠0\Omega\neq 0; and (iii) B≠0B\neq 0 and Ω≠0\Omega\neq 0. In cases (i-ii), the exchange interactions acquire geometric phase factors which in turn generate chiral spin interactions Si⋅(Sj×Sk)\textbf{S}_{i}\cdot(\textbf{S}_{j}\times\textbf{S}_{k}) and modulate the Heisenberg couplings. In case (iii), in addition to having phase factors, the exchange magnitude |Ja||J_{a}| is also exponentially renormalized, providing a knob for an orders-of-magnitude tuning of exchange scale with BB. Before turning to the technical details, we summarize our main findings below.

I.1 Summary of Main Results

(i) We first consider the case with only a magnetic field, B⁡(r)=∇r×A​(r)=B0+δ​B​(r)B(\textbf{r})=\nabla_{\textbf{r}}\times\textbf{A}(\textbf{r})=B_{0}+\delta B(\textbf{r}), where B0B_{0} is the average field [21]. We solve the multi-particle tunneling problem in the rs→∞r_{s}\to\infty limit at a fixed “Landau-level filling factor”

ν≡n⋅2​π​ℓB02=2​(ℓB0/r0)2=O⁡(1),\displaystyle\nu\equiv n\cdot 2\pi\ell_{B_{0}}^{2}=2(\ell_{B_{0}}/r_{0})^{2}=O(1), (5)

where ℓB0≡ℏ/e​B0\ell_{B_{0}}\equiv\sqrt{\hbar/eB_{0}} is the magnetic length [22]. (Throughout this paper, we assume B0≥0B_{0}\geq 0 without loss of generality.) We assume ν\nu to be of order 1 and use (ν​rs)−1≪1(\nu\sqrt{r_{s}})^{-1}\ll 1 as a small expansion parameter—which we call the “small cyclotron condition” [23]. To leading order, exchange constants are modified from their zero-field values by an Aharonov-Bohm phase factor:

ϕa​[B0]=−e​Bℏ​Σa(r)=−2ν​Σ~a(r),\displaystyle\phi_{a}[B_{0}]=-\frac{eB}{\hbar}\Sigma_{a}^{(r)}=-\frac{2}{\nu}\tilde{\Sigma}_{a}^{(r)}, (8)
Σa(r)≡∬Sa(r)d2​r=∑i12​∫ri,a(0)×d​ri,a(0)≡r02⋅Σ~a(r),\displaystyle\Sigma_{a}^{(r)}\equiv\iint_{S_{a}^{(r)}}\!\!d^{2}\textbf{r}=\sum_{i}\frac{1}{2}\int\textbf{r}_{i,a}^{(0)}\times d\textbf{r}_{i,a}^{(0)}\equiv r_{0}^{2}\cdot\tilde{\Sigma}^{(r)}_{a}, (9)

where Σa(r)\Sigma_{a}^{(r)} is the (signed) area of Sa(r)S_{a}^{(r)}, which is positive for a counter-clockwise motion. Σ~a(r)\tilde{\Sigma}_{a}^{(r)} is the dimensionless area (shown in Table 1) which is independent of rsr_{s} and ν\nu.

We note that the effects of a magnetic field on exchange constants were previously studied in Ref. [24, 25]. In particular, our calculations of the dimensionless area Σ~a(r)\tilde{\Sigma}_{a}^{(r)} in Table 1 agree with the analogous quantity sn(0)/△s_{n}^{(0)}/\triangle of Ref. [25] up to an appropriate numerical factor. However, the theoretical analysis in [25] did not properly account for the complexified path integral needed to obtain the correct asymptotic form of the exchange constants. As we will later show, the relevant tunneling trajectory is obtained by solving the complex instanton equations (44). As a result, although the leading-order expression (namely, the phase factor) in Ref. [25] coincides with our result, their subleading corrections derived there are not valid.

We first derive the exchange interactions of the WC in a magnetic field, B⁡(r)=∇r×A​(r)=B0+δ​B​(r)B(\textbf{r})=\nabla_{\textbf{r}}\times\textbf{A}(\textbf{r})=B_{0}+\delta B({\textbf{r}}),

H=∑i[pi+e​A​(ri)]22​m+∑i<je24​π​ϵ​1|ri−rj|,\displaystyle H=\sum_{i}\frac{\left[\textbf{p}_{i}+e\textbf{A}(\textbf{r}_{i})\right]^{2}}{2m}+\sum_{i<j}\frac{e^{2}}{4\pi\epsilon}\frac{1}{|\textbf{r}_{i}-\textbf{r}_{j}|}, (19)

generalizing the analogous derivation for B=0B=0 (see e.g., [18, 14]). Consider a single tunneling process PaP_{a} that cyclically permutes nan_{a} electrons at WC sites Rik\textbf{R}_{i_{k}} with spins σk\sigma_{k} to Rik+1\textbf{R}_{i_{k+1}} (ina+1≡i1i_{n_{a}+1}\equiv i_{1})

II.1 Semiclassical Limit rs→∞r_{s}\to\infty

We now obtain the large-rsr_{s} asymptotic form of Ja​[B]J_{a}[B]. This is done by first obtaining the asymptotic behavior of multi-particle propagators at an intermediate time scale

1/EDebye≪Δ​τ≪1/|Ja|,1/E_{\rm Debye}\ll\Delta\tau\ll 1/|J_{a}|, (29)

where EDebye≡e2/(4​π​ϵ​aB​rs3/2)E_{\rm Debye}\equiv e^{2}/(4\pi\epsilon a_{\rm B}r_{s}^{3/2}) sets the zero-point energy scale (per particle) of the WC. [The meaning of such time scale will become clearer later. II.2 Small Cyclotron Condition (ν​rs)−1≪1({\nu\sqrt{r_{s}}})^{-1}\ll 1

The expression (51) is valid for any value of BB [in particular, for a large field such that ν​rs=O⁡(1)\nu\sqrt{r_{s}}=O(1)], provided the complex instanton solutions of (44-45) and the resulting fluctuation determinant (41, 52) are obtained (which is a complex task). But since the B=0B=0 real instanton solutions [≡r~a(0)​(τ~)\equiv{\bf{\tilde{\textbf{r}}}}_{a}^{(0)}(\tilde{\tau})] are already known [14, 15, 18], we would like to obtain a simplified expression for JaJ_{a} by expanding r~a​(τ~){\bf{\tilde{\textbf{r}}}}_{a}(\tilde{\tau}) around r~a(0)​(τ~){\bf{\tilde{\textbf{r}}}}_{a}^{(0)}(\tilde{\tau}) in powers of 1/rs1/\sqrt{r}_{s}:

r~a​(τ~)=r~a(0)​(τ~)+1rs​δ​r~a(1)​(τ~)+O⁡(rs−1).\displaystyle{\bf{\tilde{\textbf{r}}}}_{a}(\tilde{\tau})={\bf{\tilde{\textbf{r}}}}_{a}^{(0)}(\tilde{\tau})+\frac{1}{\sqrt{r}_{s}}\delta{\bf{\tilde{\textbf{r}}}}_{a}^{(1)}(\tilde{\tau})+O\left(r_{s}^{-1}\right). (53)

Formally, this asymptotic expansion is valid when the perturbation—namely, the second term in (44)—is small compared to the unperturbed terms, i.e., when (ν​rs)−1≪1(\nu\sqrt{r}_{s})^{-1}\ll 1. We refer to this as the “small cyclotron condition” since it is equivalent to requiring that the cyclotron energy scale (ℏ​ωc=ℏ​e​B0/m)(\hbar\omega_{c}=\hbar eB_{0}/m) is much smaller than the typical oscillator energy scale (∼EDebye\sim E_{\rm Debye}) [See Footnote [23] for more detail]. In this work, we always consider the semiclassical rs→∞r_{s}\to\infty limit and work at a fixed Landau-level filling ν=O⁡(1)\nu=O(1), so that the weak-field condition is automatically satisfied. III Effects of a Berry curvature

Here, we generalize the the previous results and analyze the combined effects of a Berry curvature, Ω⁡(k)=∇k×𝓐⁡(k)=Ω0+δ​Ω​(k)\Omega(\textbf{k})=\nabla_{\textbf{k}}\times\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\textbf{k})=\Omega_{0}+\delta\Omega(\textbf{k}), and a magnetic field. For simplicity, the magnetic field is assumed to be uniform, B⁡(r)=B0=∇r×A​(r)B(\textbf{r})=B_{0}=\nabla_{\textbf{r}}\times\textbf{A}(\textbf{r}). The real-time dynamics of the 2DEG in this case is captured by the phase-space action [27, 35] 88 8 To faithfully capture the Berry curvature effect within the Hamiltonian approach (instead of the Lagrangian approach), one needs to include at least two bands as in [70, 71]. This is not necessary for our purpose as we work with the effective continuum theory.

+d​kid​t⋅𝓐(ki)]−e24​π​ϵ∑i<j1|ri−rj|+V0),\displaystyle\ \ \ +\frac{d\textbf{k}_{i}}{dt}\cdot\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\textbf{k}_{i})\bigg]-\frac{e^{2}}{4\pi\epsilon}\sum_{i<j}\frac{1}{|\textbf{r}_{i}-\textbf{r}_{j}|}+V_{0}\Bigg), (65)

where, as in (35), the Coulomb energy is measured relative to its minimum value V0=e24​π​ϵ​r0​V~0V_{0}=\frac{e^{2}}{4\pi\epsilon r_{0}}\tilde{V}_{0}.

is the single-electron energy including the coupling of the orbital magnetic moment MzM_{z} to the magnetic field, where Q0\textbf{Q}_{0} is the momentum at the band minimum. The continuum approximation near k∼0\textbf{k}\sim 0 merely results in the effective-mass renormalization m→m∗m\to m^{*} (17) with a constant shift in energy 99 9 The details of this effective-mass renormalization depends on the parent band structure from which our effective model is assumed to be derived. We do not explore such model-dependent details here, but instead treat m∗m^{*} (and MzM_{z}) as a given parameter. . This in turn renormalizes the effective Bohr radius aB∗=4​π​ϵ​ℏ2/(m∗​e2)a_{B}^{*}=4\pi\epsilon\hbar^{2}/(m^{*}e^{2}), the rsr_{s}-parameter rs∗=r0/aB∗r_{s}^{*}=r_{0}/a_{B}^{*} and the Hartree energy Eh∗=e2/(4​π​ϵ​aB∗)E_{h}^{*}=e^{2}/(4\pi\epsilon a_{B}^{*}).

In this work, we primarily focus on the spin physics in the case where only a single valley near Q0\textbf{Q}_{0} is active at low energy. In the presence of the time-reversal symmetry (TRS), valleys come in TR-related pairs at ±Q0\pm\textbf{Q}_{0} in the non-interacting band structure, with opposite Berry curvature (and opposite orbital magnetic moment). We therefore assume that the valley is fully polarized due to interactions and the TRS is spontaneously broken, so that the single-valley description with Ω≠0\Omega\neq 0 is appropriate. Within this projected single-valley theory, the term −B0​Mz​(Q0)-B_{0}M_{z}(\textbf{Q}_{0}) is constant and can be dropped without affecting the spin physics 1010 10 If multiple valleys with different orbital magnetic moments are active at low energy, then −B0​Mz​(Q0)-B_{0}M_{z}(\textbf{Q}_{0}) acts as a Zeeman-like term for valley degrees of freedom and must be retained. Relatedly, a trigonal-warping correction to the otherwise isotropic dispersion p2/2​m∗\textbf{p}^{2}/2m^{*} can drive spontaneous valley polarization of the WC even without the Zeeman-like term in (66) [53]. .

Since we are interested in thermodynamic properties, we work with the imaginary-time Euclidean action (τ=i​t/ℏ\tau=it/\hbar)

EΩ≡12​(e22​π​ϵ​r03)​ℓΩ02=Eh⋅α2​rs2\displaystyle E_{\Omega}\equiv\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{e^{2}}{2\pi\epsilon r_{0}^{3}}\right)\ell_{\Omega_{0}}^{2}=E_{h}\cdot\frac{\alpha}{2r_{s}^{2}} (74)

is much smaller than the Debye energy scale EDebyeE_{\rm Debye} 1212 12 Here, EΩE_{\Omega} could be understood as the quantum zero-point energy scale associated with the harmonic oscillator V=12​Ktyp​(X2+Y2)V=\frac{1}{2}K_{\rm typ}(X^{2}+Y^{2}), where Ktyp∼e22​π​ϵ​r03=d2d​r2​e24​π​ϵ​r|r=r0K_{\rm typ}\sim\frac{e^{2}}{2\pi\epsilon r_{0}^{3}}=\frac{d^{2}}{dr^{2}}\frac{e^{2}}{4\pi\epsilon r}\Big|_{r=r_{0}} is the appropriate “spring constant” for the Coulomb interaction. Since we work with the effective Lagrangian within a single band, the band-projected position operators do not commute due to the presence of a Berry curvature, [X,Y]≈i​Ω​(k)[X,Y]\approx i\Omega(\textbf{k}) [27, 72, 73]. IV Discussion

We analyzed how a magnetic field BB and a Berry curvature Ω\Omega modify the exchange interactions in a Wigner crystal (WC) via an asymptotic large-rsr_{s} expansion. When either BB or Ω\Omega is present individually, the effect is simply to multiply the exchange constant Ja(0)J_{a}^{(0)} at B=Ω=0B=\Omega=0 by a phase factor: the Aharonov-Bohm phase ϕa​(B)\phi_{a}(B) for B≠0B\neq 0 (6-9) and the Berry phase γa​(Ω)\gamma_{a}(\Omega) for Ω≠0\Omega\neq 0 (12-15). When both are present, in addition to having both phases, the exchange magnitude |Ja​[B,Ω]|=Ja(0)​(Eh∗,rs∗)|J_{a}[B,\Omega]|=J_{a}^{(0)}(E_{h}^{*},r_{s}^{*}) is also modified via an effective-mass renormalization (17) originating from the coupling of the orbital magnetic moment to BB.

In the absence of BB and Ω\Omega, the WC is thought to occur for rs≳37r_{s}\gtrsim 37 [5], aside from the subtleties of possible intermediate phases [6]. (This critical rsr_{s} value will generally shift when BB or Ω\Omega is finite.) Fig. 2 shows that for rs≤80r_{s}\leq 80, at least four processes, J3J_{3}, J2,J_{2}, J4J_{4} and J6J_{6}, are appreciable, yielding a highly frustrated generalized Heisenberg model. To the best of our knowledge, the phase diagram of this J2J_{2}-J3J_{3}-J4J_{4}-J6J_{6} model in the presence of the Aharonov-Bohm and Berry phase (7,13,16) has not been systematically explored. By contrast, the simpler J2J_{2}-J3J_{3}-J4J_{4} model for B=Ω=0B=\Omega=0 (i.e., ϕa=γa=0\phi_{a}=\gamma_{a}=0) has been studied in [42, 43, 44, 45, 46]. For a non-zero BB or Ω\Omega, the J2J_{2}-J3J_{3}-J4J_{4} model [J5=J6=J6′=0J_{5}=J_{6}=J_{6}^{\prime}=0 in (3)] becomes 1414 14 The effective spin Hamiltonian in the lattice model (as opposed to the continuum model of the present work) in the presence of a magnetic field is analogously derived in [74, 75]. The chiral spin interaction χi​j​k\chi_{ijk} can also arise in metals as demonstrated in [76].

Notably, chiral interactions on   \mathord{\vbox{\hbox{\hbox to8.07pt{\vbox to7.27pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 4.03404pt\lower-2.77283pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke=#000000} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill=#000000} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=0.4pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{}{{}}{}{{{}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}{}{}{}{}}\lxSVG@fill\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 4.77 M 1.45 4.77 C 1.45 5.57 0.8 6.22 0 6.22 C -0.8 6.22 -1.45 5.57 -1.45 4.77 C -1.45 3.97 -0.8 3.31 0 3.31 C 0.8 3.31 1.45 3.97 1.45 4.77 Z M 0 4.77}{stroke:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces {}{{}}{}{{{}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}{}{}{}{}}\lxSVG@fill\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M -4.13 -2.38 M -2.68 -2.38 C -2.68 -1.58 -3.33 -0.93 -4.13 -0.93 C -4.93 -0.93 -5.58 -1.58 -5.58 -2.38 C -5.58 -3.19 -4.93 -3.84 -4.13 -3.84 C -3.33 -3.84 -2.68 -3.19 -2.68 -2.38 Z M -4.13 -2.38}{stroke:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces {}{{}}{}{{{}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}{}{}{}{}}\lxSVG@fill\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 4.13 -2.38 M 5.58 -2.38 C 5.58 -1.58 4.93 -0.93 4.13 -0.93 C 3.33 -0.93 2.68 -1.58 2.68 -2.38 C 2.68 -3.19 3.33 -3.84 4.13 -3.84 C 4.93 -3.84 5.58 -3.19 5.58 -2.38 Z M 4.13 -2.38}{stroke:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces {}{{}}{} {}{} {}{} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 4.77 L -4.13 -2.38 L 4.13 -2.38 Z}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces } \lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}}}, next-nearest-neighbor Heisenberg exchanges and four-spin terms hi​j​k​lh_{ijkl} are each known to stabilize the Kalmeyer-Laughlin chiral spin liquid (CSL) [48, 49, 45]. Since all of them are present here, the CSL phase may arise over a broad parameter range in a WC in the presence of BB and/or Ω\Omega.

Recent experiments report an extended region of the WC phase in rhombohedral multilayer graphene (RMG) [50, 51], suggesting that our results may be directly relevant to the WC and proximate correlated phases in this system. For concreteness, we provide a rough estimate of the exchange energy scale using data from the tetra-layer device [52]. We take the interlayer potential difference between the top and bottom layer to be Δ=90​meV\Delta=90{\,\rm meV} (for which the band structure becomes most flat), the carrier density ne=0.4×1012​cm−2n_{e}=0.4\times 10^{12}{\,\rm cm^{-2}} and the relative permittivity ϵr≈5\epsilon_{r}\approx 5. From the band structure calculation shown in Fig. 12 (a) of [52], the effective mass and Fermi energy at this density are roughly m∗/me≈3m^{*}/m_{e}\approx 3 and EF≈1​meVE_{F}\approx 1{\,\rm meV}, respectively. These parameters yield an effective Hartree energy Eh=m∗/meϵr2​(27.2​eV)≈3.3​eVE_{h}=\frac{m^{*}/m_{e}}{\epsilon_{r}^{2}}(27.2{\,\rm eV})\approx 3.3{\,\rm eV}, an effective Bohr radius aB=ϵrm∗/me​(5.29×10−11​m)≈8.8×10−11​ma_{B}=\frac{\epsilon_{r}}{m^{*}/m_{e}}(5.29\times 10^{-11}{\rm m})\approx 8.8\times 10^{-11}{\rm m} and an average inter-particle distance r0=1/π​ne≈8.9×10−9​m.r_{0}=1/{\sqrt{\pi n_{e}}}\approx 8.9\times 10^{-9}{\rm m}. The resulting Coulomb energy scale is ECoulomb∼Eh​aBr0≈33​meVE_{\rm Coulomb}\sim E_{h}\frac{a_{B}}{r_{0}}\approx 33{\,\rm meV}, corresponding to an interaction parameter rs≡ECoulomb/EF∼30​–​40.r_{s}\equiv E_{\rm Coulomb}/E_{F}\sim 30\text{--}40. The effective exchange scale thus is Jeff∼Eh​e−rs​Srs5/4∼0.1​–​0.01​K,J_{\rm eff}\sim E_{h}\frac{e^{-\sqrt{r_{s}}S}}{r_{s}^{5/4}}\sim 0.1\text{--}0.01{\,\rm K}, where we took S≈1.5S\approx 1.5 (Table 1). By contrast, the valley ordering in the WC arises in the large-rsr_{s} limit from the trigonal warping at order Veff∼Eh/rs3V_{\rm eff}\sim E_{h}/r_{s}^{3} [53], which evaluates to Veff∼1​KV_{\rm eff}\sim 1\,{\rm K}. Therefore, in rhombohedral graphene, valley ordering of the WC occurs at a temperature scale orders of magnitude larger than that of spin ordering, Jeff≪VeffJ_{\rm eff}\ll V_{\rm eff}. Moreover, since the spin gg-factor in RMG is close to the bare electron value (=2)(=2), a magnetic field larger than B∼Jeff2​μB∼0.1​–​0.01​TB\sim\frac{J_{\rm eff}}{2\mu_{B}}\sim 0.1\text{--}0.01{\,\rm T} is sufficient to fully polarize the spin degrees of freedom.

Taken together, our work shows how a magnetic field and Berry curvature modify the magnetic properties of a quantum crystal, in particular by generating chiral spin terms that can stabilize the chiral spin-liquid phase. More broadly, our work highlights that the effects of those geometric phases manifest fundamentally differently in strongly correlated continuum systems as compared to weakly interacting systems or Hubbard-type lattice models.

Note added: Upon completion of this work, Ref. [54] appeared, which partially overlaps with this work. The results are largely in agreement where they overlap.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
